newsitem.title: USA: Boeing to seek U.S. help if EU blocks merger.
newsitem.headline: Boeing to seek U.S. help if EU blocks merger.

text.p: Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp., unwilling to concede Europe's authority to derail their proposed merger, are ready to ask the U.S. government for help if necessary.
Nonetheless, the companies are cooperating with the European Union as it investigates their proposed combination.

But if the EU tries to block the merger, "that gets to be just not an issue for Boeing Co., it's also an issue for the U.S. government," said Raymond Waldmann, vice president of international business for Boeing in Seattle.
"You have to look at the agreement between the United States and the European Commission with respect to who has primacy in deciding merger issues," he said.
At this point, it is unclear how Washington might respond. But Boeing officials may get questions about the EU involvement at the company's annual shareholders meeting in Seattle Monday.
The top EU official reviewing the merger dislikes it, in particular because Boeing has exclusive-provider agreements with Delta Air Lines Inc. and AMR Corp.'s American Airlines.
"I can't see how possibly we can give our authority to the merger with such a system in place," European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said during a recent visit to Washington.
Airbus Industrie, a consortium of European manufacturers, is hurt by the agreements. But Van Miert casts the issue in broader terms, suggesting a general concern about competition.
The EU will give Boeing a list of its specific concerns with the merger in May and make a final decision on the case in July.

If the EU does not approve, it could impose a fine of 10 percent of Boeing's annual gross income worldwide. But Boeing Chief Executive Phil Condit has expressed confidence the company will work out its differences with the EU.
Boeing's Waldmann said that, if the EU did try to halt the merger, he would expect the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and the State and Defence departments to become involved.

The Federal Trade Commission is reviewing the legality of the merger. The Defence Department will advise it, because Boeing and McDonnell Douglas are heavily involved in the production of military airplanes, space launch vehicles and other defence equipment.
At best, any problems would slow final resolution of the deal, which Condit initially predicted would be approved by mid-summer.
The U.S. government awaits massive amounts of Boeing paperwork and is nowhere near deciding to approve, reject or restructure the merger.

Only after the U.S. government has considered the case might it work with European competition authorities. In the past when the Americans and the EU have proposed different remedies to unacceptable deals, they have sometimes been able to settle on a joint approach.
Nonetheless, some American experts say there are fundamental differences in the way the two competition authorities operate.

These Americans characterise U.S. antitrust authorities as relatively independent but see the 20 European commissioners -- whose job is to act in the EU's interest -- as more responsive to political and economic influences.
"The antitrust laws are a national religion in the United States but that's not the case in Europe," said an American antitrust lawyer with an international practice, who asked not to be identified.
Boeing strongly reflects that American perspective, suggesting the EU is looking over its shoulder at the effect on Airbus.
"The presumption that they have jurisdiction because it has an effect on their industry is what we think drives the commission's competition review," said Boeing's Waldmann.
